items.followUp: State Charles’ Law and write its mathematical expression.

rubric.why: States the inverse relationship between pressure and volume under the required conditions.
rubric.description: States Boyle’s Law: for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, volume is inversely proportional to pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the conditions and inverse relationship, or an equivalent statement of the law.

rubric.why: Gives the mathematical expression of Boyle’s Law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either equivalent expression.

modelAnswer: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, its volume is inversely proportional to its pressure.
Mathematically: PV = constant, or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? Give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies water as the solvent in an aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Defines an aqueous solution as one in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for indicating that the solute is dissolved in water.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a solute dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example such as salt or sugar dissolved in water.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
Example: sodium chloride dissolved in water (salt water).

items.followUp: Define molar concentration and state its unit.

rubric.why: Defines concentration in terms of solute amount in a specified volume of solution.
rubric.description: Defines concentration as the amount of solute present in a unit volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, allowing equivalent wording.

rubric.why: Names a commonly used unit for concentration.
rubric.description: States a unit of concentration, such as mol dm⁻³ or g dm⁻³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either a correct unit and its appropriate name or notation.

modelAnswer: Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a unit volume of solution.
A common unit is mole per cubic decimetre (mol dm⁻³).

items.followUp: State one difference between an element’s atomic number and its mass number.

rubric.why: Identifies valency as an element’s combining capacity and distinguishes it from a signed oxidation state.
rubric.description: Defines valency as the combining capacity of an atom or ion; it is written without a sign.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or the valid distinction that valency has no sign.

rubric.why: Identifies oxidation state as a signed value representing an atom’s apparent charge in a compound or ion.
rubric.description: Defines oxidation state as the apparent charge assigned to an atom, which may be positive, negative, or zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or the signed nature of oxidation state.

modelAnswer: Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or ion and is written without a sign.
Oxidation state is the apparent charge assigned to an atom and may be positive, negative, or zero.

items.followUp: Why is chlorine classified as a non-metal?

rubric.why: Links oxygen’s electron configuration or tendency to gain electrons with non-metal behaviour.
rubric.description: Oxygen has six electrons in its outermost shell and tends to gain two electrons to complete that shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its six valence electrons or its tendency to gain two electrons.

rubric.why: Gives the resulting behaviour or ion characteristic of oxygen as a non-metal.
rubric.description: Oxygen forms negatively charged oxide ions or shares electrons in covalent bonds, characteristic of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating oxide-ion formation or covalent bonding.

modelAnswer: An oxygen atom has six electrons in its outermost shell and tends to gain two electrons to complete it.
It forms negatively charged oxide ions (O²⁻), a characteristic of non-metals.

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of lithium greater than that of sodium?

rubric.why: Explains the difference in atomic size and shielding between sodium and potassium.
rubric.description: Sodium has a smaller atomic radius and less shielding than potassium, so its outer electron is closer to the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the smaller radius, less shielding, or closer outer electron explanation.

rubric.why: Connects the stronger nuclear attraction to the greater energy needed to remove sodium’s outer electron.
rubric.description: The outer electron in sodium is held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it than in potassium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stronger attraction or greater energy-to-remove conclusion.

modelAnswer: Sodium has a smaller atomic radius and fewer occupied electron shells than potassium, so its outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
The nucleus attracts sodium’s outer electron more strongly; therefore, more energy is needed to remove it.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size generally decreases from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in nuclear charge across a period.
rubric.description: Across a period, nuclear charge increases as the number of protons increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that nuclear charge increases.

rubric.why: Explains that stronger attraction makes electron loss less likely, so electropositivity decreases.
rubric.description: The stronger attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons makes atoms less likely to lose electrons; hence electropositivity decreases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the increased attraction to decreased tendency to lose electrons or decreased electropositivity.

modelAnswer: From left to right across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell.
The stronger attraction makes atoms less likely to lose electrons, so electropositivity decreases.

items.followUp: Write any five characteristics of a compound.

rubric.why: Recognizes that a mixture has variable composition.
rubric.description: The components of a mixture may be present in any proportion; its composition is not fixed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mixture composition or component proportions can vary.

rubric.why: Identifies that mixing does not remove the components’ individual properties.
rubric.description: Each component retains its own properties in a mixture.

rubric.why: Identifies physical separation as a way to separate mixture components.
rubric.description: The components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating physical separability or giving a valid physical separation method.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a mixture from a substance formed by chemical combination.
rubric.description: The components are not chemically combined with one another.

rubric.why: Recognizes that mixtures do not have a fixed chemical formula or definite characteristic melting or boiling point.
rubric.description: A mixture has no definite chemical formula and generally does not have a fixed melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid characteristic not already counted.

modelAnswer: A mixture has a variable composition; its components may be present in any proportion.
The components retain their individual properties.
The components can be separated by physical methods.
The components are not chemically combined.
A mixture has no definite chemical formula or fixed melting or boiling point.
